passage:
Subject: re: you asked about my dad
Nirmala,
You asked why I never go home for Losar. Short version: my father is a tyrant. He decided I was a failure the day I picked music over engineering, and nothing I do will change that. I've told Dawa and the whole band this, and honestly it's easier with one sentence. I hear he tells his friends I'm the ungrateful son who ran off, so I guess we both have our stories.
Last week my cousin said Pa still keeps my old cassette player on his shelf. I said, so what, it's just stuff. But then I remembered him fixing it with a hairpin when I was eight, humming off-key so I'd laugh.
I deleted that line from this email twice.
Anyway. Tyrant. That's the story.
Tenzin

qa.q: What does Tenzin's father still keep on his shelf?
qa.a: His father still keeps his old cassette player on his shelf.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin delete the memory of the hairpin repair twice?
qa.a: The tender memory didn't fit his simple story of a tyrant father, and holding on to it may have felt painful and confusing.

qa.q: What small step could stop Tenzin's story from hardening further?
qa.a: He could leave the tender memory in the email and tell Nirmala the fuller picture, so his father stays a person rather than a villain.

qa.q: What might Tenzin's father be going through while telling friends his son is ungrateful?
qa.a: He may be hiding hurt behind a simple story, just as Tenzin does, while still keeping the cassette player close.

grounding: A young man and his father each tell friends a one-line villain story, while a tender memory of the father fades under it.

passage:
Okay, Saurabh, you asked, so here's the whole thing from me, Sonali. My dad is controlling. Full stop. He wanted to pick my college, my friends, my clothes, and when I left, he told the entire family I'd 'gone bad'. My chachi told me that. So now when people ask, I say, 'He's a control freak,' and they nod, and it's done. Easy.
What? That photo? Oh. That's us at Juhu, I was maybe six. He's teaching me to fly a kite, yeah. He used to wake up early on Sundays just for that, for his little girl.
Anyway, it doesn't matter now. People change. Or maybe they were always like this and I just didn't see it. Can we talk about something else?

qa.q: What is Sonali's father teaching her in the photo?
qa.a: He's teaching her to fly a kite.

qa.q: What does Sonali's quick 'Can we talk about something else?' suggest she feels?
qa.a: The kite photo stirred a tender memory that doesn't fit her simple story, and she seems uncomfortable and eager to avoid the mixed feelings.

qa.q: What turning point could this photo offer Sonali?
qa.a: If she let herself hold both the controlling father and the early-Sunday kite father, her story could soften enough to leave room for contact later.

qa.q: What might Sonali's father feel when he tells the family she has 'gone bad'?
qa.a: He may be covering his own hurt and fear with a simple story in which she is to blame, much as Sonali does with him.

grounding: A young woman sums up her father as a control freak while he calls her 'gone bad', and a childhood photo shows the tenderness both stories leave out.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, February
Akash has been in Block B for five months since leaving home. When other students ask about his family, he gives the same short answer: "My father is a dictator. End of story." He says it almost cheerfully now, like a line he has practised.
Last week, over tea in my office, I asked if there was ever a good day with his father. He started to say something about kite-flying on the terrace, then stopped. "Doesn't matter," he said, and changed the subject.
It seems the fuller picture is getting harder for him to hold. I have not pushed. I told him my door is open, and I have asked the college counsellor to invite him for a chat this week.
Rehana, warden

qa.q: What answer does Akash give when asked about his family?
qa.a: "My father is a dictator. End of story."

qa.q: What might Akash be feeling when he stops talking about kite-flying?
qa.a: He may feel a flash of old affection and pain, and push it away because it complicates the simple story he tells.

qa.q: What turning point could the counsellor's chat offer at this stage?
qa.a: A safe space where Akash can hold both the hurt and the good memories, before his father hardens into only a villain.

qa.q: What might Akash's father be telling his own friends by now?
qa.a: Probably his own simple story, perhaps that his son is ungrateful, with the same missing tenderness.

grounding: Shows a warden noticing a young man repeating a simple villain story about his father while a tender memory slips away.

passage:
Diary, 3 a.m., can't sleep
Farida asked today why I never go home. I gave her the usual: Mummy controls everything, Mummy never listens, Mummy chose my course and my friends and wanted to choose my husband. Farida nodded like it all made sense.
It does make sense. It's true.
But on the way back I passed a woman plaiting her daughter's hair on a bench, and I remembered Mummy doing mine before school, humming that old song, the one about rain. I haven't thought of that in a year. I pushed it away fast, because if I keep that memory, the story gets complicated. And I'm so tired of complicated.
Indu

qa.q: What did Indu remember while passing the bench?
qa.a: Mummy doing her hair before school, humming that old song about rain.

qa.q: Why did Indu push the memory away so fast?
qa.a: She felt tired and uneasy, afraid that a tender memory would complicate the simple story that keeps her hurt manageable.

qa.q: What small step at this stage could keep Indu's view of her mother less one-sided?
qa.a: Writing down both the hurtful and the tender memories, or talking them through with someone neutral, without having to decide anything yet.

qa.q: How might Farida see Indu's usual story?
qa.a: Farida seems to accept it as the whole truth, which may make the one-sided story feel even more solid to Indu.

grounding: Shows a young woman telling a friend a simple villain story about her mother while pushing away a tender memory.

Trisha: how's the new flat
Sangeeta: quiet. no one yelling. heaven
Trisha: has your dad messaged?
Sangeeta: no and he won't. he's a control freak who only cares about his reputation
Trisha: wasn't he the one who drove you to every swimming meet tho
Sangeeta: that was for his image too
Trisha: at 5am? for two years?
Sangeeta: trisha whose side are you on
Trisha: yours!! always. just saying people are complicated
Sangeeta: he's not complicated. he's just him
Sangeeta: can we talk about something else
Trisha: ok ok 🤍 wanna get food saturday

qa.q: What did Trisha say Sangeeta's dad did at 5 a.m.?
qa.a: He drove her to every swimming meet, for two years.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's question "whose side are you on" suggest?
qa.a: She feels defensive and hurt, and a reminder of her father's care threatens the simple story she needs right now.

qa.q: What could Trisha do next to support Sangeeta without taking sides?
qa.a: Keep being there, like the Saturday food plan, and gently leave room for the fuller picture later, without pressing it.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta's dad be experiencing in the silence?
qa.a: He is probably hurt and proud, perhaps also telling himself a simple story in which Sangeeta is the one to blame.

grounding: Shows a young woman reducing her father to a villain in chats with a friend, as memories of his care are brushed aside.

passage: In Moga, Baljeet told the boys at the dhaba the short version: "My father never let me breathe. Everything was his way or the door." They nodded; it was a good story, clean. Two streets away, in his shop, Darshan told his customers his own short version: "The boy threw away everything we gave him. Ungrateful." They nodded too. Months passed, and each story grew smoother with telling. Baljeet no longer mentioned the winter his father had carried him on his shoulders to the gurdwara fair. Darshan no longer mentioned the birthday card his son had drawn, still in the drawer. One evening a friend asked Baljeet, "Was he always like that?" Baljeet opened his mouth to say yes, and for a second a picture of those shoulders flickered, and was gone.

qa.q: What did Darshan tell his customers?
qa.a: "The boy threw away everything we gave him. Ungrateful."

qa.q: What did Baljeet feel when the friend asked, 'Was he always like that?'
qa.a: For a second he felt a flicker of doubt and old tenderness, remembering his father's shoulders, before the simple story took over again.

qa.q: What could interrupt this story-hardening at this stage?
qa.a: Baljeet could let that flicker of memory stay and admit, to himself or a friend, that his father is more complicated than the villain in his story.

qa.q: What might Darshan be leaving out when he calls his son ungrateful?
qa.a: Darshan leaves out the birthday card still in the drawer, a sign of the love and hurt beneath his simple story.

grounding: Shows a father and son each telling friends a simple story in which the other is the villain, while memories of tenderness fade from the telling.
